abstract: We release an urgency dataset that consists of English tweets relating to natural crises. The set is annotated along with annotations of their corresponding urgency status. Additionally, we release evaluation datasets for two low-resource languages, i.e. Sinhala and Odia, and demonstrate an effective zero-shot transfer from English to these two languages by training cross-lingual classifiers. We adopt cross-lingual embeddings constructed using different methods to extract features of the tweets, including a few state-of-the-art contextual embeddings such as BERT, RoBERTa and XLM-R. We train a variety of classifier architectures, supervised and semi supervised, on the extracted features. We also further experiment with ensembling the various classifiers. With very limited amounts of labeled data in English and zero data in the low resource languages, we show a successful framework of training monolingual and cross-lingual classifiers using deep learning methods which are known to be data hungry. Specifically, we show that the recent deep contextual embeddings are also helpful when dealing with very small-scale datasets. Classifiers that incorporate RoBERTa yield the best performance for the English urgency detection task, with 25% F1 score absolute improvement over the baselines. For the zero-shot transfer to low resource languages, classifiers that use LASER features perform the best for Sinhala transfer while XLM-R features benefit the Odia transfer the most.

bibliographic.title: Detecting Urgency Status of Crisis Tweets: A Transfer Learning Approach for Low Resource Languages
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics

content.problem: Urgency signals in social media posts during crises could support humanitarian response, but automatic language technology does not exist for most of the world's languages, and labeled urgency data is largely absent for low-resource languages such as Sinhala and Odia.
content.proposed_solution: The authors release new English, Sinhala, and Odia tweet urgency datasets and train monolingual and zero-shot cross-lingual classifiers over contextual and projection-based cross-lingual embeddings, strengthened with self-training pseudo-label augmentation and classifier ensembling.
content.algorithm_or_model: Embedding-feature classifiers (MLP, CNN, SVM, RF) with self-training data augmentation and ensemble voting over RoBERTa, LASER, XLM-R, VecMap, and ProcB features
dataset_testbed: English crisis tweet urgency dataset (1,919 annotations created by the authors on Figure-Eight)
Sinhala urgency evaluation dataset (LORELEI IL10, LDC2018E57, 181 natively annotated sentences)
Odia urgency evaluation dataset (LORELEI IL11, LDC2019E62, 510 natively annotated sentences)
Unlabeled crisis-related tweets from the Imran et al. (2016) disaster tweet collection used for self-training augmentation
English-Sinhala (415,042 sentences) and English-Odia (454,540 sentences) parallel corpora from LDC LORELEI packages used to build projection-based cross-lingual embeddings

content.claim: Contextual deep embeddings make urgency detection feasible even with very small labeled data, with RoBERTa-based classifiers giving the best English performance (a 25-point absolute F1 gain over the baselines), and zero-shot transfer succeeds to Sinhala and Odia, where LASER features work best for Sinhala and XLM-R features best for Odia.
author_stated_limitations: Fine-tuning the pre-trained contextual models visibly degrades performance when the downstream dataset is very small, so frozen extracted features were used instead.
The semi-supervised augmentation does not necessarily improve performance when the pseudo-labels come from classifiers trained on very limited labeled data.
Synthetic data helps only when the training and evaluation label distributions are similar, improving the Odia classifiers but not the Sinhala ones.

evidence.problem_quote: However, with the existence of more than 7,000 languages worldwide, automated human language technology does not exist for many languages. A possible solution to this problem is to transfer models learned in high resource language settings such as English to low resource languages (Ruder et al., 2019).
evidence.proposed_solution_quote: To this end, we collect and release English, Sinhala and Odia urgency datasets that consist of tweets relating to natural crises, annotated with urgency status. To demonstrate that we are able to effectively transfer the task of urgency detection from English to low-resource languages, we use English annotated tweets for training, and Sinhala/Odia annotated tweets for evaluation only, therefore, exploring zeroshot transfer.
evidence.claim_quote: Specifically, we show that the recent deep contextual embeddings are also helpful when dealing with very small-scale datasets. Classifiers that incorporate RoBERTa yield the best performance for the English urgency detection task, with 25% F1 score absolute improvement over the baselines.
author_stated_limitation_quotes: We tried fine-tuning these pre-trained models and found that the performance deteriorates evidently in the case where the down-stream task has a very small dataset (Goodfellow et al., 2016);

The semi-supervised approach of augmenting the dataset does not necessarily boost the performance even further in the case when the pseudo-labels are generated by classifiers that are trained on limited resources.

Adding synthetic data consistently improves the performances of the classifiers for Odia but not for Sinhala (if we consider macro F1-score). We suspect that synthetic data might help the task if the label distribution of the training dataset is similar to that of the evaluation dataset.
